entries.topicDescription: Creating domain-specific languages using Kotlin's builder pattern.

tips.title: Building a type-safe HTML DSL
tips.content:
Kotlin DSLs combine lambdas with receivers, extension functions,
and operator overloading to create readable, type-safe mini-languages.

The compiler ensures you can only nest valid elements.
You can't put a <td> directly inside a <html> — the types prevent it.

Popular Kotlin DSLs: Ktor routing, Gradle Kotlin DSL, Compose UI,
kotlinx.html, and Exposed (SQL).

tips.title: @DslMarker — scoping DSL receivers
tips.content:
Without @DslMarker, nested lambdas can access outer receivers implicitly.
This leads to confusing bugs where you call a method on the wrong scope.

@DslMarker creates an annotation that restricts implicit receiver access.
Members of the outer receiver are hidden inside inner lambdas —
you must use explicit 'this@outer' to access them.

Always use @DslMarker in production DSLs to prevent scope leaking.

tips.title: Lambda with receiver — the DSL foundation
tips.content:
A lambda with receiver lets you call methods on an object inside a lambda
as if you were inside that class. The receiver becomes 'this'.

This is the core mechanism behind Kotlin DSLs and builder patterns.
Functions like apply, with, and buildString all use this concept.

Signature: ClassName.() -> Unit means "a lambda where 'this' is ClassName."

tips.title: buildString, buildList and buildMap are DSLs in the standard library
tips.content:
Several standard-library functions take a lambda with receiver so you can build a value with a small local DSL: buildString gives you a StringBuilder, buildList a MutableList, and buildMap a MutableMap. The block runs once and the function returns the finished, read-only result.

They are the simplest way to see the pattern in action, and a good default when building a value takes loops or conditions.

tips.title: Keep the builder mutable and the result immutable
tips.content:
A DSL block needs something it can change as it runs, so the builder class has var properties and mutable collections. The value it produces should not: build() copies that state into an immutable object (a data class with val properties and read-only collections) and that is what the rest of the program sees.

This keeps the flexibility of the DSL where it is used and the safety of immutability everywhere else, and it stops code from changing the object after construction.

tips.title: Use operator invoke to nest configuration blocks
tips.content:
An operator function named invoke lets you call an object or a string like a function, and with a trailing lambda that looks like a block. Declared as a member extension on String, it lets a DSL open a nested block with just a name and braces.

This is how DSLs get their outline-like structure. Because nested blocks can call functions of the outer receiver by accident, pair this style with @DslMarker for larger DSLs.

tips.title: infix functions make assertion-style DSLs read like sentences
tips.content:
An infix function with one parameter can be called without the dot and parentheses. That is enough to write test assertions or rules that read almost like English: result shouldBe expected, age isBetween 18 and 65.

Restraint helps: infix suits a few well-named operations with an obvious meaning. Too many of them make code cryptic, and the parser needs care when several infix calls are combined without parentheses.

tips.title: Gradle's Kotlin DSL is lambdas with receiver
tips.content:
build.gradle.kts is ordinary Kotlin code. android { } and dependencies { } are functions that take a lambda with receiver, so inside the block you can call the receiver's members without a prefix. The implementation(...) inside dependencies { } is a generated extension function on that receiver.

That explains why the IDE can autocomplete and check the build script: it is type-checked Kotlin, not a separate configuration language. It is also why you can call normal Kotlin (variables, loops, functions) in a build script.

tips.title: Composable lambdas form a UI DSL
tips.content:
Jetpack Compose UI is built with the same language features as any DSL: trailing lambdas for children, lambdas with receiver (a Column content lambda has a ColumnScope receiver, so it can use Modifier.weight), and named arguments with defaults for options.

Nested layouts read like the structure of the screen, and a scope receiver makes only valid calls available in the right place: weight is offered inside a Row or Column, not everywhere.

tips.title: Don't build a DSL when named arguments and defaults are enough
tips.content:
A DSL adds code to write and maintain: builder classes, receivers, and often a marker annotation. It pays off when a structure is nested or repeated (HTML, routes, UI, build scripts). For a flat set of options, named arguments and default values do the job with no extra machinery.

Ask whether callers will nest blocks or build a variable amount of structure. If not, a data class with defaults is simpler, easier to test and easier to discover.
tips.codeSnippet:
// A DSL would be overkill for this
data class Notification(
    val title: String,
    val body: String = "",
    val priority: Int = 0,
    val sound: Boolean = true
)

val n = Notification(title = "Saved", priority = 1)
